narrative_summary.historical_use: Roselle calyces, reported in the literature as Hibiscus sabdariffa, are used as sour beverages and in traditional medicine in Africa and Asia; this history is distinct from clinical evidence [2][6].
narrative_summary.modern_application: Draft research profile: roselle calyx infusions have been studied for blood-pressure outcomes, with substantial preparation and study-quality limitations [1][2]. In a double-blind trial of 65 adults aged 30–70 years with prehypertension or mild hypertension who were not taking blood-pressure medicines, a six-week calyx-tea regimen reduced systolic pressure more than placebo; the diastolic difference was not significant [1]. A review of 17 chronic trials found a systolic-pressure signal but very high heterogeneity (I²=95% in the placebo comparison); this supports a conservative Level B for the studied blood-pressure outcomes, not proven cardiovascular-event prevention or medication equivalence [2]. A 25-man acute crossover study improved flow-mediated dilation without a significant blood-pressure reduction [4]. Pending manual scientific review. Numeric medicinal doses are omitted because product and population details must be assessed together.
narrative_summary.side_effects: Mild, transient gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in one trial summarized by the review; short trials and incomplete reporting cannot establish long-term safety or rare-event rates [2]. Hypersensitivity is a regulatory contraindication [6].
narrative_summary.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to roselle or related Malvaceae is listed by EDA [6]. Low blood pressure and concurrent blood-pressure treatment warrant precautionary clinical assessment because additive effects are plausible [2][6]. Medicinal use in children is insufficiently characterized in these sources. EDA includes a precaution to stop two weeks before planned surgery because of possible glucose effects; a clinical perioperative benefit of that interval has not been established [6].

clinical_data.used_part: Fleshy red calyces, usually dried and infused in water; tea and concentrated extracts have different constituent exposures. Clinical sources use the synonym Hibiscus sabdariffa [1][5][6].
primary_active_compounds: Hibiscus acid and related organic acids [6]
clinical_data.mechanism_of_action: Animal and in-vitro work summarized in the review investigates angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), vascular calcium influx and endothelial nitric-oxide signaling; these hypotheses do not establish clinical ACE inhibition or explain all human effects [2]. Human flow-mediated dilation improved in one small acute trial, but nitric-oxide and blood-pressure changes were not significant [4].

pharmacokinetics.absorption: In six healthy volunteers given a single Hibiscus extract, measured intact anthocyanins peaked in plasma at a median 1.5 hours. These abstract-level, compound-specific findings cannot describe absorption of the complete botanical or establish calyx-product dosing [3].
pharmacokinetics.distribution: Human tissue distribution and protein binding of complete calyx extracts were not established in the selected sources [2][3].
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: A small human crossover trial detected circulating gallic acid and methylated phenolic acids after an aqueous calyx drink; complete metabolic pathways and clinically relevant CYP effects remain unresolved [4].
pharmacokinetics.excretion: In six volunteers, 0.018% of the administered total anthocyanins was recovered as measured intact anthocyanins in urine within seven hours. This is not total recovery of all metabolites; extract-level clearance and impairment adjustments are unknown [3].

safety_and_interactions.drug_interactions: Additive hypotension with antihypertensive drugs is a precautionary pharmacodynamic concern [2][6]. EDA also flags chloroquine, simvastatin and diabetes medicines, but this extraction has not independently verified the underlying clinical interaction studies; direction and magnitude must not be assumed [6]. A hydrochlorothiazide interaction described in the review was in rats and is not an established human interaction [2].
safety_and_interactions.toxicity: No reliable long-term human toxicity threshold is established. Short trial tolerability and animal toxicity results do not establish safety during chronic concentrated-extract use [2].

special_precautions.pregnancy: Insufficient human pregnancy safety data; EDA does not recommend medicinal use during pregnancy [6].
special_precautions.lactation: Milk transfer and infant safety are unknown; EDA does not recommend medicinal use during breastfeeding [6].
special_precautions.hepatic_impairment: No validated hepatic-impairment dosing or safety studies identified in the selected sources; concentrated-extract exposure requires individual clinical assessment [2][6].
special_precautions.renal_impairment: No validated renal-impairment dosing data identified in these sources; potential blood-pressure and diuretic effects warrant individualized assessment with concurrent medicines. This is a precautionary inference, not an impairment-specific clinical finding [2][6].

narrative_summary.historical_use: Rose hip, seed and combined hip-and-seed preparations are described as traditional medicinal materials in the pharmacological review. Their different composition and preparation should be distinguished; traditional use is not proof of clinical benefit [3].
narrative_summary.modern_application: Draft research profile: a particular rosehip seed-and-husk powder has been investigated for osteoarthritis pain, with small manufacturer-supported studies limiting confidence [1][2]. A meta-analysis of three trials (287 participants; median duration three months) found a small pain-score benefit, but all trials were supported by the same manufacturer and independent replication was requested [1]. A double-blind crossover study enrolled 94 patients with hip or knee osteoarthritis and compared seed-and-husk powder with placebo for three months per period [2]. Evidence is provisionally Level B for pain outcomes with that studied preparation, not all rosehip teas, oils, species mixtures or products. Other uses remain insufficiently established [3][4]. Pending manual scientific review. Full-text quality appraisal remains pending; no numeric dose is given.
narrative_summary.side_effects: Adverse-event frequencies, rare events and long-term safety are not established by the accessible abstracts. The meta-analysis specifically calls for further efficacy and safety evaluation [1]. Absence of a detailed adverse-event table in an abstract is not absence of adverse effects [1][2].
narrative_summary.contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to the product is a precautionary reason to avoid exposure. Other specific contraindications, pediatric safety and perioperative washout intervals could not be established from the selected sources; no validated interval is proposed [1][3].

clinical_data.used_part: The clinical evidence concerns powder made from the seeds and shells/husks of a Rosa canina subspecies. Seed oil, seed-free hip material, teas and multi-species rosehip blends are not interchangeable with this powder [2][3].
primary_active_compounds: Lipophilic constituents investigated in rosehip/seed pharmacology; specific clinical standardization not established in the accessible abstracts [3]
clinical_data.mechanism_of_action: The pharmacological review describes antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects involving lipophilic constituents in experimental preparations. A clinically established receptor or enzyme target and proof that these mechanisms cause pain changes are lacking; mechanistic evidence must not be equated with disease modification [3].

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Human absorption parameters for the studied complete powder were not established in the selected sources [1][3].
pharmacokinetics.distribution: Human tissue distribution and protein binding for the studied powder were not established [3].
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Human metabolite and clinically meaningful CYP interaction profiles for the studied powder were not established [3].
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Human clearance, half-life and renal/biliary recovery of the complete powder were not established [3].

safety_and_interactions.drug_interactions: No clinically quantified herb–drug interaction or validated CYP interaction profile was established in the selected sources. This is an evidence gap rather than proof of no interaction; concurrent medication and product composition require individual assessment [1][3].
safety_and_interactions.toxicity: Long-term toxicity, rare hepatic or renal events and maximum tolerable exposure are unresolved. The three-trial pain meta-analysis does not establish broad safety of other rosehip preparations [1].

special_precautions.pregnancy: Pregnancy safety for the studied medicinal powder could not be established from the selected sources; this is an evidence gap, not proof of fetal safety or harm [1][3].
special_precautions.lactation: Milk transfer and infant safety for the studied medicinal powder could not be established from the selected sources; an evidence-based safety recommendation cannot be made here [1][3].
special_precautions.hepatic_impairment: No hepatic-impairment study or validated dose adjustment was identified in the selected sources [1][3].
special_precautions.renal_impairment: No renal-impairment study or validated dose adjustment was identified in the selected sources [1][3].

narrative_summary.historical_use: Pelargonium root preparations have a documented tradition of use for respiratory complaints; the EMA common-cold indication is based on long-standing traditional use, rather than a finding of well-established clinical efficacy. The EMA monograph covers P. sidoides and/or P. reniforme [1][6].
narrative_summary.modern_application: Draft research profile: proprietary Pelargonium root extracts have been investigated for acute cough and respiratory symptoms, but certainty and formulation differences remain substantial [1][2][3]. The Cochrane review judged evidence low for acute bronchitis and very low for common cold or sinusitis, with suspected publication bias and differences between liquids and tablets [1]. A later meta-analysis of 11 EPs 7630 trials (2195 participants) reported cough improvement; the authors include manufacturer employees or paid consultants, and the analysis does not remove the limitations or establish interchangeability with other products [3]. A UK feasibility trial recruited 134 adults and demonstrated recruitment feasibility rather than definitive efficacy [2]. Archive classification is Level U for a firm clinical efficacy conclusion and Level T for EMA traditional common-cold use [1][6]. Pending manual scientific review. Study regimens describe research exposure and are not dosing advice.
narrative_summary.side_effects: EMA 2024 lists gastrointestinal complaints, nasal or gum bleeding, hypersensitivity including anaphylaxis, rash, pruritus, urticaria, angioedema, hepatitis and hepatotoxicity, with frequency unknown [6]. The Cochrane trials reported more adverse events with extract than placebo, without serious events in those trials [1]. Liver causality remains disputed: a case reassessment found none of 15 reports probable or highly probable, but this does not negate current regulatory warnings [4][6].
narrative_summary.contraindications: Hypersensitivity is an EMA contraindication. Signs of liver injury require stopping the product and medical assessment [6]. The 2024 monograph does not recommend oral use below age three. For its dry-extract preparations b) and c), children under six should receive only liquid dosage forms; a dry extract and a solid finished dosage form are different concepts. Symptoms persisting longer than one week or worsening require medical advice [6]. No evidence-based perioperative washout interval was established in this extraction.

clinical_data.used_part: Root; clinical findings mainly concern proprietary EPs 7630 liquid/dry extracts. EMA describes defined ethanol-extracted preparations and also covers P. reniforme, so genus-level and mixed-species preparations cannot be assumed equivalent to P. sidoides trial material [2][3][6].
primary_active_compounds: Root extract is a mixture; no single clinically proven active constituent accounts for the symptom findings [1][3]
clinical_data.mechanism_of_action: Experimental work summarized by the EPs 7630 review investigates host-defense signaling, including interferon and tumor necrosis factor, alongside antiviral and mucociliary effects. These are primarily preclinical hypotheses; they do not establish antiviral treatment efficacy, prevention of complications or a clinically validated molecular target [3].

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Human constituent-specific absorption and absolute bioavailability were not established in the selected clinical sources; EMA traditional-use monograph does not provide pharmacokinetic parameters [1][6].
pharmacokinetics.distribution: Human tissue distribution and protein binding of whole root extracts remain insufficiently characterized in the selected sources [6].
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Complete human metabolic pathways and clinically relevant CYP effects were not established in the selected sources [6].
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Validated whole-extract half-life, renal clearance and impairment adjustments are unavailable in the selected sources [6].

safety_and_interactions.drug_interactions: EMA reports no interactions, which is not proof that all combinations are safe [6]. Nasal and gingival bleeding are reported adverse reactions; a clinically quantified interaction with anticoagulants or antiplatelets was not established in this extraction. Medication review remains prudent [6].
safety_and_interactions.toxicity: Hepatitis and hepatotoxicity reports remain in current EMA warnings even though causality was not substantiated in one reassessment [4][6]. A manufacturer-sponsored, non-interventional 2026 study enrolled 300 adults (298 completing) and reported no clinical signs of liver injury after a seven-day PELARGO capsule course. Short follow-up and symptom-based surveillance cannot rule out rare, delayed or asymptomatic injury [5]. Product-specific findings cannot establish long-term safety of all root extracts.

special_precautions.pregnancy: Safety in pregnancy is not established and EMA does not recommend medicinal use [6].
special_precautions.lactation: Milk transfer and infant safety are unknown; EMA does not recommend medicinal use during breastfeeding [6].
special_precautions.hepatic_impairment: No validated impairment adjustment identified. Reported hepatitis/hepatotoxicity warrants particular caution in existing liver disease and immediate medical assessment of possible liver-injury symptoms [6].
special_precautions.renal_impairment: No validated renal-impairment adjustment or adequate disease-specific safety data identified in selected sources [6].

narrative_summary.historical_use: Linseed has long been used as a bulk-forming laxative; EMA distinguishes well-established use of seed for habitual constipation from traditional demulcent use for mild gastrointestinal discomfort [5].
narrative_summary.modern_application: Draft research profile: flaxseed products have been studied for bowel function and blood-pressure outcomes, with seed, oil and lignan extracts representing different interventions [1][2][5]. A 2023 meta-analysis of 33 trials (2427 participants) reported modest pooled blood-pressure reductions but very high heterogeneity (I² above 92%); the archive uses conservative Level B for the studied pressure outcomes rather than generalizing to every product [1]. An earlier analysis also found formulation-dependent results [2]. EMA recognizes seed as a bulk laxative, while demulcent use is traditional (Level T); regulatory well-established use is not itself an archive Level A clinical-trial score [5]. A separate triple-blind trial studied flaxseed regimens for 12 weeks, but its abstract gives inconsistent participant totals, so it is not used for a precise sample-size or effect claim [4]. Pending manual scientific review. No numeric medicinal dose is given here.
narrative_summary.side_effects: EMA lists flatulence as common and hypersensitivity including anaphylaxis-like reactions as very rare. Insufficient fluid can cause choking, oesophageal blockage or intestinal obstruction; excessive seed exposure can cause abdominal discomfort and flatulence [5]. NCCIH also notes bloating, fullness and diarrhea with higher exposures [6].
narrative_summary.contraindications: EMA contraindicates hypersensitivity, swallowing/throat disorders, intestinal narrowing or obstruction/ileus, megacolon and certain unexplained bowel symptoms, including rectal bleeding or persistent sudden bowel-habit changes. Medicinal use under age 12 is not recommended; EMA also cautions against use in women with hormone-dependent tumours [5]. A validated perioperative washout interval was not identified.

clinical_data.used_part: Dried ripe seeds, whole/broken or milled, and seed mucilage. Seed oil lacks the same bulk-forming fibre exposure; purified lignan extracts have a separate pharmacokinetic and safety evidence base [3][5][6].
clinical_data.mechanism_of_action: For bowel effects, water-binding mucilage increases intestinal content volume and softens stool, with stretch-related effects on transit; this is a local bulk mechanism described by EMA, not a receptor-specific systemic action [5]. Blood-pressure mechanisms are not conclusively assigned to a single constituent in the human meta-analyses [1][2].

pharmacokinetics.absorption: In healthy postmenopausal women given purified flax lignan extracts, secoisolariciresinol peaked at approximately 5–7 hours; enterodiol and enterolactone appeared later. These results describe SDG-derived compounds, not whole-seed mucilage or seed oil [3].
pharmacokinetics.distribution: Human tissue distribution of complete seed products was not established in the selected sources; purified-lignan serum exposure does not establish all tissue concentrations [3].
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: SDG is hydrolyzed to secoisolariciresinol and converted by intestinal bacteria to enterodiol and enterolactone [3]. Some seed bulk material is fermented to short-chain fatty acids while some is passed in stool [5].
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Human SDG studies measured urinary lignans and reported approximate serum half-lives of 4.8 hours for secoisolariciresinol, 9.4 hours for enterodiol and 13.2 hours for enterolactone; these cannot define whole-seed clearance or impairment dosing [3].

safety_and_interactions.drug_interactions: EMA warns that linseed can delay intestinal absorption of medicines and specifies separation of at least half to one hour. Co-use with motility-suppressing medicines such as opioids or loperamide requires medical supervision because of obstruction risk [5]. NCCIH describes anticoagulant/antiplatelet interactions as theoretical, not established clinical bleeding interactions [6].
safety_and_interactions.toxicity: NCCIH advises against eating raw or unripe seeds because of potentially toxic constituents; seed preparation matters [6]. EMA identifies obstruction risk when fluid intake is inadequate and incomplete reproductive/genotoxicity/carcinogenicity testing. No universal long-term toxicity threshold can be inferred from short supplementation trials [5][6].

special_precautions.pregnancy: Medicinal pregnancy safety is not established and EMA does not recommend use; NCCIH notes inconclusive possible pregnancy risk. This does not equate medicinal preparations with ordinary food exposure [5][6].
special_precautions.lactation: Milk transfer and infant safety are insufficiently characterized; EMA does not recommend medicinal use while breastfeeding [5][6].
special_precautions.hepatic_impairment: No validated hepatic-impairment adjustment for medicinal seed or lignan extract was established in the selected sources [3][5].
special_precautions.renal_impairment: No validated renal-impairment adjustment is established. Fluid-dependent bulk use requires individual assessment when fluid intake is restricted; this is a precaution rather than a tested dosing rule [5].

narrative_summary.historical_use: Horse chestnut seed extracts have been traditionally used for pain, swelling and other complaints. EMA distinguishes specific standardized oral extracts with well-established use in venous insufficiency from traditional oral/topical preparations for minor venous complaints or bruises [3][4].
narrative_summary.modern_application: Draft research profile: standardized horse chestnut seed extracts have been studied for short-term venous-insufficiency symptoms, with larger and longer rigorous trials still needed [1]. A Cochrane review of 17 trials found signals for reduced leg pain and leg volume but emphasized caveats [1][3]. A randomized, partially blinded 12-week trial of 240 adults compared a dried seed extract with compression stockings and placebo; leg-volume findings do not establish prevention of thrombosis or equivalence for every clinical outcome [2]. Provisional archive Level B applies to studied short-term venous symptoms. Raw seeds and other raw parts are toxic and are not the tested preparations [4]. Pending manual scientific review. No numeric medicinal dose is given here.
narrative_summary.side_effects: Standardized oral seed extracts may cause gastrointestinal complaints, headache, vertigo/dizziness, itching or allergic reactions; EMA gives frequency as unknown. Topical preparations may cause skin hypersensitivity [3][4]. Short-term trial tolerability cannot exclude rare or delayed adverse events [1].
narrative_summary.contraindications: Hypersensitivity is an EMA contraindication. Sudden leg swelling, severe pain, thrombophlebitis, ulcers, skin inflammation or possible cardiac/renal insufficiency require medical evaluation rather than self-treatment [3]. Oral venous-use preparations are not recommended below age 18 in the EMA monograph. Raw seed, leaf, bark and flower ingestion must be avoided [3][4]. No validated perioperative washout interval was established.

clinical_data.used_part: Seed-derived standardized extracts used in clinical trials; not raw seeds, bark, leaves or flowers. EMA standardized extracts specify constituent assay and extraction solvent, so older aescin values and newer protoaescigenin-based values should not be casually interchanged [1][3][4].
primary_active_compounds: Aescin/escin (mixture of triterpene saponins in standardized seed extracts) [1][2][3]
clinical_data.mechanism_of_action: The exact mechanism is unknown. EMA describes preclinical and clinical pharmacological evidence involving venous tone and capillary filtration; these are pharmacological processes rather than established single molecular targets, and symptom evidence does not imply antithrombotic efficacy [3].

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Relevant human absorption parameters for the specified whole extract are not supplied by the EMA monograph; formulation-specific bioavailability cannot be inferred from symptom trials [3].
pharmacokinetics.distribution: Human tissue distribution and protein binding for complete standardized extracts were not established in the selected sources [3].
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Complete human metabolic pathways and clinically relevant CYP effects were not established in selected sources [3].
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Reliable extract-level renal/biliary recovery, half-life and impairment adjustment were not established in the selected sources [3].

safety_and_interactions.drug_interactions: EMA reports no interactions for the defined preparations; this is not proof that all products or drug combinations lack interactions. A clinically quantified anticoagulant or CYP interaction was not established in the selected sources, so no severity grade or washout interval is invented [3].
safety_and_interactions.toxicity: Raw seeds, bark, flowers and leaves contain a toxic component and are unsafe for oral use. NCCIH distinguishes these from standardized seed extracts in which that component has been removed [4]. The evidence concerns short exposures, often no longer than 12 weeks; reproductive, genotoxicity and carcinogenicity testing is incomplete and long-term human toxicity remains uncertain [3][4].

special_precautions.pregnancy: Pregnancy safety is not established; EMA does not recommend use [3].
special_precautions.lactation: Milk transfer and infant safety are unknown; EMA does not recommend use during breastfeeding [3].
special_precautions.hepatic_impairment: No validated hepatic-impairment dose adjustment or adequate disease-specific safety data identified; individualized assessment is required [3].
special_precautions.renal_impairment: EMA specifically calls for medical evaluation in renal insufficiency or unexplained leg oedema; no validated renal dosing adjustment is established [3].
